title: Traditional Indian Diet and Daily Walks Put 60.9% of Early Diabetes Patients Into Remission
excerpt: A six-month programme of familiar Indian food in measured portions and 40 minutes of daily walking achieved remission in 53 of 87 adults with recent-onset type 2 diabetes — in a single-arm study its own authors say now needs a controlled trial.
body:
• In a six-month study of 87 adults with type 2 diabetes diagnosed within the previous two years, 60.9% achieved remission — HbA1c below 6.5% at least three months after stopping glucose-lowering medication — on a traditional Indian diet plus daily exercise.
  • The programme used familiar foods — multigrain chapati, dal, sprouts, green leafy vegetables, nuts and fruit — at about 1,200 kcal a day, with 40 minutes of walking and 10 minutes of deep breathing daily. Average weight fell 4.67 kg and average HbA1c dropped from 7.32% to 6.27%.
  • Walking mattered most: participants who completed the routine on at least 80% of days had 8.24 times the adjusted odds of remission of those who followed it less closely.
  • Caution for readers: this was a single-arm study with no control group, and participants stopped medication only under close medical supervision. Do not stop or change diabetes medication on your own — discuss any diet change with your doctor first.

A traditional Indian plate, eaten in measured portions, combined with a daily walk put six in ten adults with early type 2 diabetes into remission within six months, a study from two Maharashtra centres has found. The research, conducted by the Chellaram Diabetes Institute in Pune and Dr Kale's Diabetes and Psychiatry Clinic in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar and published in Diabetes & Metabolic Syndrome: Clinical Research & Reviews, tested whether a culturally familiar diet could do what very low-calorie and highly restrictive diets have done in earlier remission trials.

What the study did

The prospective, single-arm study enrolled 87 adults whose type 2 diabetes had been diagnosed within the previous two years; 75 completed the six-month intervention. Participants followed a Local Healthy Moderate Carbohydrate (LHMC) diet of about 1,200 kcal a day — roughly 500 kcal below their baseline intake — built from multigrain chapatis, lentils, sprouts, green leafy vegetables, nuts and fruit in defined portions, with carbohydrate at 44–46% of energy, protein 25–30% and fat 25–30%. Alongside the diet came structured daily exercise: 40 minutes of walking and 10 minutes of deep breathing. Glucose-lowering medications were discontinued when the intervention began, under medical supervision, and remission was defined strictly — an HbA1c below 6.5% measured at least three months after stopping medication. The full methods and results are on the study's PubMed record.

"Our patients did not need special foods, skipped meals or fasting windows. They ate the traditional Indian food their families eat, in measured portions, and walked every day. Six in ten reached remission without any diabetes medicine, and those who walked most consistently did best."

— Dr Vedavati Purandare, Chellaram Hospital Diabetes Care and Multispecialty

The results

Fifty-three participants achieved remission, an estimated rate of 60.9%. Average weight fell by 4.67 kg, and average HbA1c declined from 7.32% to 6.27%. Continuous glucose monitoring was more favourable in the remission group, with researchers reporting glucose in the normal range 90.7% of the time among those in remission against 85.5% among the rest. The clearest predictor was exercise adherence: participants who followed the walking routine on at least 80% of days had 8.24 times the adjusted odds of achieving remission compared with those with lower adherence. The researchers describe this as the first demonstration of remission rates above 60% in recent-onset type 2 diabetes using a moderate-calorie, moderate-carbohydrate Indian diet and a walking-based regimen, rather than the very low-calorie diets that dominate existing remission trials.

What the study cannot tell us — yet

The limits matter as much as the headline number. There was no control group, so the study cannot separate the effect of the intervention from what structured follow-up, monitoring and motivation alone might achieve; the authors themselves call the findings hypothesis-generating and say they warrant confirmation in controlled studies. The follow-up was six months, so it does not show how many participants stay in remission over years. Dr A. G. Unnikrishnan, CEO and endocrinologist at Chellaram Hospital, put the caution plainly: "A larger controlled trial must now confirm these findings, and patients should change their treatment only with consultation with their doctor."

What this means if you have early type 2 diabetes

For Indian and diaspora readers, the practical reading is narrow but real. If your diabetes was diagnosed recently, this study adds evidence — not yet proof — that a familiar, home-cooked Indian diet in controlled portions, plus a daily 40-minute walk you actually keep up, is a serious option to discuss with your doctor, including whether a supervised trial of reducing medication is appropriate in your case. What it does not support is stopping medication unsupervised: every participant in this study stopped medication inside a monitored programme with glucose tracking. Bring the study to your next appointment — its PubMed record carries the abstract, the remission definition and the trial registration (CTRI/2023/08/056621) — and let the decision be a medical one.
